ME-2024-LD1040.s: Starting July 1, 2026, the yearly cost-of-living increase for retirement pay would apply to up to $40,000 of benefits for retired state employees and teachers who retired on or before June 30, 2011, or to their beneficiaries. The change would raise the amount of pension pay that can get the increase each year. It affects those retirees and their beneficiaries in Maine's state retirement system.

ME-2024-LD1056.s: The bill would say that prepaid wireless phone service is subject to Maine sales tax, and it would add a plain definition for that kind of service. It would also say that this service is not subject to the state service provider tax. The change would apply back to sales on or after July 1, 2022, but taxes already paid before the effective date would not be refunded or credited.

ME-2024-LD1061.s: The bill would give $1,563,470 from the General Fund each year in 2025-26 and 2026-27 to the Department of Health and Human Services. The money would help the Maine Child Abuse Prevention Councils support families and provide child abuse prevention services across the state. It was written as an emergency measure, so it would take effect when approved.

ME-2024-LD1099.s: The bill would exempt disposable and reusable diapers from Maine sales tax, including diaper covers, wraps, and fasteners used with reusable diapers. The change would begin on January 1, 2026. It would affect diapers marketed for adults or children.

ME-2024-LD1111.s: The bill would give one-time state funding of $10 million to the Kennebec Water District. The money would help expand water service lines in Fairfield for residents whose private wells were affected by PFAS, a group of chemicals linked to water contamination.

ME-2024-LD1211.s: This bill would change sales tax rules for some rented equipment and vehicles. It would narrow the definition of “automobile” so some pickup trucks and vans count only if they are not used mainly to haul goods or freight. It would also change what counts as a lease or rental for property used only at the lessor’s main business location.

ME-2024-LD1219.s: The bill would raise state funding for each University of Maine System campus based on a comparison to similar schools, starting at 95% for fiscal year 2026-27 and 100% for fiscal year 2027-28. It would also set the system’s minimum hourly wage at 125% of the state minimum wage starting July 1, 2025. The bill includes state funds of $14,371,274 for 2025-26 and $24,526,974 for 2026-27.

ME-2024-LD1252.s: The bill would change the rules for the Maine Agriculture, Food System and Forest Products Infrastructure Investment Advisory Board and the fund it oversees. It would limit grants to producers that have, or are trying to build, a processing or manufacturing facility in Maine, and would require the money to support that facility and related equipment or supply chain needs. It would also bar board members from voting on a matter when they have a conflict of interest, meaning a direct personal financial stake for themselves or an immediate family member.

ME-2024-LD13.s: The bill would create a state fund in the Secretary of State’s office to pay for making and delivering election materials, like ballots, absentee ballot envelopes, and voter forms. It would move $266,000 from the state’s general surplus each year starting in 2025, with that amount adjusted every two years for cost of living. It would also bring back a working group to study schools used as polling places and have the department report its findings and recommendations by December 15, 2025.

ME-2024-LD140.s: The bill would raise Maine’s homestead property tax exemption for eligible homeowners. Starting with property tax years on or after April 1, 2026, the exemption would grow by $10,000 each year until it reaches $85,000, with annual inflation adjustments starting in 2033. It affects people who qualify for the homestead exemption.

ME-2024-LD1443.s: The bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to keep paying certain service providers, such as behavioral health agencies and housing help groups, at their old contract rate if a new contract is delayed more than 30 days. It would also require the department to pay the extra costs and interest on loans or credit lines that providers use because of these delays. It would apply to providers in good standing with the department.

ME-2024-LD1528.s: The bill would create a separate account to help fund public-private work for Maine’s Working Farmland Access and Protection Program. It would also move $1,000,000 from the state’s general surplus to support farmland conservation efforts. The bill would add one full-time staff position in the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry.

ME-2024-LD1639.s: The bill would require each school in Maine to provide at least 900 instructional hours each school year, starting with the 2026-2027 school year. It defines instructional hours as regular school time for teaching and school-led learning, not lunch, recess, or after-school clubs, and it lets the education commissioner grant a waiver for emergencies like disasters or public health events. School units would also have to file yearly reports showing they meet the rule, and the state could take action if they do not.

ME-2024-LD1720.s: The bill would give long-term care workers, including nurses, certified nursing assistants, direct care workers, and housekeeping and dietary staff, access to the state retirement system and state health plan. It would also require MaineCare to pay nursing homes and residential care facilities for staff training and interpreter services, including training for nurse aide work, direct care work, and English as a second language. The Department of Professional and Financial Regulation would have to offer the written nursing assistant exam in French, Spanish, Cantonese, Mandarin, and Filipino by January 1, 2026.

ME-2024-LD1764.s: The bill would set minimum staff-to-student ratios for career and technical education centers and regions in Maine, with one ratio for sites with fewer than 1,000 students and another for larger sites. It would also let a center or region use a different ratio if it fits the program’s industry standard and the Education Commissioner approves it. Starting in 2025, centers and regions would have to report funding gaps each year, and the Department of Education would use available funds to help meet the staffing rules, with preference for smaller programs.

ME-2024-LD1847.s: The bill would set up testing rules for medical cannabis and cannabis products, including checks for contamination, THC levels, and correct labeling. It would require dispensaries and caregivers to test products before selling or giving them to patients, and it would require records of those tests. It would also set rules for how samples are collected and when tested products can be sold again without new testing.

ME-2024-LD1888.s: This bill would create a new crime of racketeering in Maine. It would apply when a person is tied to a criminal group and takes part in at least two listed crimes, such as drug trafficking, human trafficking, theft, fraud, gambling, arson, or murder. It would also let the state seize assets linked to racketeering and set rules for where these cases can be brought. The bill is an emergency measure and would take effect when approved.

ME-2024-LD191.s: For tax years starting on or after January 1, 2025, partnerships and S corporations could choose to pay Maine income tax at the entity level. Owners and members would get a credit equal to 90% of their share of that tax, and some nonresident members could be exempt from filing a Maine return if the entity pays the tax. The bill would also let Maine adopt rules to carry out this new tax system.

ME-2024-LD192.s: The bill would let certain utility vehicles qualify for a state sales tax refund when they are used in commercial fishing, farming, aquaculture, or wood harvesting. A utility vehicle here means a small work vehicle with a bed that moves cargo and can go 20 to 50 miles per hour. If enacted, it would take effect on January 1, 2026.

ME-2024-LD195.s: The bill would create a state program to certify some small businesses in farming, fishing, and wood harvesting for a tax break tied to special savings accounts. These accounts would be used only to save money for business equipment or other capital expenses, and withdrawals not used for that purpose would count as taxable income. Contributions could be made from January 1, 2026 through December 31, 2029, and each account could hold up to $250,000.

ME-2024-LD1980.s: The bill would create a Law Enforcement Retention Advisory Council to advise the Public Safety commissioner on ways to improve police recruitment, retention, and wellness. It would also require death certificates to show whether a person had worked as a police officer, firefighter, or emergency medical worker. In addition, it would add wellness training and critical incident debriefing to basic law enforcement training and fund one wellness coordinator position at the Maine Criminal Justice Academy.

ME-2024-LD1996.s: The bill would change the rules for general assistance and clarify the state’s role in the program. It would remove a requirement that the Department of Health and Human Services give municipal overseers access to a real-time online database used to check if someone qualifies for help. It would also update the department’s reporting rules to include more data on who gets aid, what it is used for, and local poverty and benefit use.

ME-2024-LD2066.s: The bill would create the Child Care Employment Award, a state program that gives child care help to workers at licensed child care centers and family child care homes whose own children use licensed care. The help would be paid directly to the care provider, and the Health and Human Services Department could set rules on award amounts, waiting lists, quality standards, and how many children can be helped. It would also add one full-time staff job to run the program and provide $3,000,000 in funding for the 2026-27 year.

ME-2024-LD2115.s: The bill would rename a state fund and use it to test and address pollution in private drinking water wells. It would let the money pay for testing, cleanup, filter systems, water line hookups, and bottled water for wells affected by hazardous substances, including PFAS. The Department of Environmental Protection would set the rules for who can get help, and the bill includes $1 million in general fund money for 2026-27.

ME-2024-LD2121.s: The bill would let certain public officials, like judges, lawmakers, and top state officers, and some close family members ask to keep their home addresses out of some public records and online records. It would create an Office of Information Privacy in the Department of the Secretary of State to review these requests and manage the process. State, county, and city offices would have to remove or stop sharing the address after approval, with some records and court-ordered releases still allowed.

ME-2024-LD2151.s: The bill would give $4 million in fiscal year 2026-27 to help federally qualified health centers build or improve pharmacy services for people in rural and underserved areas. It would support things like licensed retail pharmacies, buying and delivering drugs under the federal 340B discount program, and improving pharmacy sites or equipment. The health department would set up the application process and make the first awards by December 15, 2026.

ME-2024-LD2159.s: This emergency measure would require school buses to have crossing arms and for drivers to use them while the bus is stopped to pick up or let off passengers. If a driver does not use the arm, it would be a Class E crime. The Secretary of State would also have to revoke that driver's school bus endorsement for at least 2 years.

ME-2024-LD2237.s: The bill would let police use oral fluid tests, along with blood, breath, and urine tests, to check for alcohol or drug use in some OUI cases. It applies to aircraft operators and people who hunt, and the text also covers watercraft, snowmobile, and ATV cases. It would also let these test results be used as evidence in court under the same general testing rules.

ME-2024-LD260.s: This resolution would ask voters to amend the Maine Constitution to bar the state and local governments from denying equal rights based on race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, disability, ancestry, or national origin. It would affect Maine residents and state and local governments. If approved by voters, the change would become part of the state constitution.

ME-2024-LD326.s: The bill would raise the property tax break for Maine residents who are legally blind. It would increase the exempt value of their home from $4,000 to $10,000. The change would apply to property tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2026.

ME-2024-LD328.s: Beginning January 1, 2026, the state would pay 100% of Medicare Part B premiums under Medicare Advantage for some retired state employees and retired teachers. It would apply only if the retiree is not eligible for federally approved Medicaid services. For retired teachers, the payment would be made through the Maine Education Association benefits trust plan.

ME-2024-LD461.s: The bill would fund 4 Maine State Trooper jobs and related costs to do rural patrols in Washington County. It would use General Fund money of $315,788 in 2025-26 and $325,477 in 2026-27, and Highway Fund money of $170,040 in 2025-26 and $175,257 in 2026-27. Because it is an emergency bill, it would take effect when approved.

ME-2024-LD462.s: The bill would change Maine retirement rules so some state retirement members could get service credit for time served in the U.S. Armed Forces during operations in Lebanon and Grenada. It affects members of the Maine Public Employees Retirement System who served during those conflict periods. The Lebanon dates are August 21, 1982 to February 26, 1984, and the Grenada dates are October 25, 1983 to December 15, 1983.

ME-2024-LD500.s: The bill would require free water testing for low-income residents with private household wells, including tests for arsenic and other contaminants, plus PFAS, which are man-made chemicals. It would also direct the state to tell people about free testing and about grants for water treatment systems. The bill would make clear that homeowners whose well water is over state limits for PFAS and other listed contaminants can get those grants.

ME-2024-LD519.s: The bill would repeal Maine rules that set up a pooled market for individual and small group health plans, so those plans would no longer have to be offered through that market. It would also remove related rules for clear choice plan designs and some rate review steps tied to the pooled market. The bill would end a related reinsurance program rule for the Maine Guaranteed Access Reinsurance Association when a pooled market is operating.

ME-2024-LD527.s: The bill would create bail officers in the judicial branch to help set and carry out bail under Maine law. It would let bail officers, along with bail commissioners, set preconviction bail in many cases, while keeping limits for murder cases, some serious crimes, and domestic violence cases. It would also set training rules and allow a bail commissioner fee of up to $60, with exceptions for people who cannot pay.

ME-2024-LD534.s: The bill would require professional investigators to tell crime victims and witnesses why they are asking questions, who their client is, and whether the person may benefit from the work. It would also require them to say that the victim or witness does not have to talk to them. If a victim, witness, or a minor’s parent or guardian asks them to stop, they could not keep contacting that person unless given permission.

ME-2024-LD549.s: The bill would set up a statewide system to track sexual assault forensic exam kits and would require state agencies, hospitals, labs, police, and district attorneys to use it. It would also change how long kits are stored, require many kits to be sent to the Maine State Police Crime Laboratory for testing starting January 1, 2027, and give victims anonymous access to track their kit. The bill would also require the state to report on kit counts and testing times each year.

ME-2024-LD593.s: The bill would provide ongoing funding for the Land for Maine’s Future Trust Fund for eligible expenses and other allowed uses. It sets General Fund money at $10 million in 2025-26 and $10 million in 2026-27.

ME-2024-LD696.s: The bill would provide one-time funding for the Maine Teacher Residency Program at the University of Southern Maine. It would set aside $1 million from the General Fund for 2025-26.

ME-2024-LD748.s: The bill would increase funding for Maine’s Bridging Rental Assistance Program. It would provide $660,000 in general fund money in 2025-26 and $660,000 in 2026-27. The money is meant to help more people on the waiting list get housing vouchers, including people living with mental health challenges.

ME-2024-LD836.s: Would authorize a $50 million state bond issue to help pay for upgrades to municipal culverts at stream crossings. The money would fund a competitive grant program that matches local funds for projects that improve fish and wildlife habitat and help towns prepare for floods and storms. Eligible applicants would include local governments, municipal conservation groups, soil and water conservation districts, and private nonprofit groups, and voters would have to approve the bond before it could take effect.

ME-2024-LD838.s: This concept draft would explore ways to save money for electric customers by using public financing and public ownership of electric transmission and distribution lines. It affects the state’s electric utility delivery system.

ME-2024-LD875.s: The bill would provide state funding for essential services for victims of domestic violence. It would give the Department of Health and Human Services $4 million in fiscal year 2025-26 and $4 million in fiscal year 2026-27 for these services. It would take effect when approved.
